notes.claim: A TDR uses the radar principle: a pulse goes down the cable and changes in impedance send reflections back, which are displayed as a map of the cable.
A positive reflection shows a higher impedance and a negative one a lower impedance, because conductors moving apart or closer together change the impedance.
An open conductor shows a large positive trace and a short circuit a negative trace. A joint shows a small positive followed by a small negative trace.
A wet splice or water gives a short positive and negative trace, and your notes list a ragged trailing section for water ingress.

The velocity factor is the ratio of the pulse speed in the cable to the speed of light, and it must be set for the cable. If unknown, test a known length and adjust it until the displayed end distance is correct.
Megger lists a velocity factor of 0.54 to 0.62, which is 162 to 186 m per microsecond, for power XLPE cable.
Distance comes from the time of the reflected pulse times the velocity, taking half of the time, because the pulse goes to the fault and back. Your notes write L = t × v ÷ 2.
If the velocity factor is wrong for the cable, the displayed distance will be wrong.

A clear open reflection is not necessarily the end of the cable, because it can also be a break or cut, so the end is proved with open and linked tests. Linked gives a negative peak, open a positive one.
TDR needs two separate conductive elements, one of which may be the armour or screen. Your notes say two conductors in parallel, a fixed 50 V pulse, and shorter pulse width for shorter cables.
Testing from both ends and recording the distance to fault helps work out how wide a problem is, and after water the velocity factor changes, so readings past the water may be wrong.
Your notes say TDR only works on low resistance faults, typically under 100 Ω (200 Ω for Teleflex), with accuracy of 0 to 1% of cable length.
